videos.script: Most people write the code first and the tests afterwards, if there is time left. Test-driven development turns that round. {{title}} You write one small test. You run it and watch it fail. Then you write just enough code to make it pass. Then you tidy up, while every test stays green. {{cycle}} Red, green, refactor. One turn takes a minute or two, not an afternoon. {{minutes}} In this lesson you build the library's fine calculator that way. Its first version returns a constant, and that is on purpose. {{fake}} A second example forces the real formula out of it. A third catches an early return that would have charged a member a negative fine. {{examples}} Then comes the step people skip. The refactor, where the design improves with the tests as a net. {{refactor}} Writing the test first also changes the design. A function that reads today's date from the clock is hard to test, so the test asks for the date as an argument. {{design}} And none of this is free. The last section says where the method struggles, and what happened when researchers measured it. {{struggles}}
